The Advanced Medical Technology Association (AdvaMed) DME Work Group appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Request for Information (RFI) within the proposed rule...
analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Advanced Medical Technology Association (AdvaMed)
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association (trade association representing medical device, diagnostic, digital health technology, and health information system manufacturers)
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** World's leading trade association for medical technology; members range from largest to smallest medtech producers including hundreds of small companies with fewer than 20 employees; signed by Zoe Guengerich, Senior Director, Payment & Healthcare Delivery Policy

---

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

AdvaMed's comment focuses on two discrete areas: (1) the DMEPOS prior authorization RFI, where it describes the significant administrative and patient care burden of current manual, fragmented PA processes and recommends standardization, API connectivity, automation, and device manufacturer access to CMS APIs; and (2) the proposed Open Payments "failure to report" definition, where AdvaMed raises serious concerns about statutory authority overreach, inadequate IP/trade secret protections, lack of good faith negotiation procedures, insufficient contractor confidentiality obligations, and failure to protect privileged materials from CMP exposure.

---

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP, GENERAL (DMEPOS PA RFI)
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 42 C.F.R. § 403.902 (proposed "failure to report" definition); 42 C.F.R. § 403.912 (audit authority); 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7h(a) and (b)(1)(A) (Open Payments statute); 45 C.F.R. §§ 160.402, 160.420, 160.422 (HIPAA enforcement); 45 C.F.R. § 5.65(d) (FOIA predisclosure); 91 Fed. Reg. 19890; 91 Fed. Reg. at 19985-19986
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR-based APIs (referenced in context of industry pledge and API connectivity); CAQH Index Report 2024 (cited for ePA adoption statistics)

---

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: DMEPOS PA – Current Burden on Patients and Providers**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL (DMEPOS PA RFI)
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** DMEPOS PA delays are particularly problematic because patients need prompt access for mobility, respiratory function, and chronic disease management. As of 2024, only 35% of medical plans have adopted electronic PA standards; 43% use payer-specific portals; 22% rely on manual processes. Variation in documentation requirements across payers causes differing criteria, documentation standards, submission methods, and review processes, driving avoidable denials. Delayed authorization creates financial exposure for suppliers who must dispense items without authorization.
- **Specific request:** Standardize documentation requirements and minimum data elements across payers; require machine-readable PA rules; require clear actionable denial reasons; define service-level expectations for payer response times.

**Topic 2: DMEPOS PA – Automation and Technology Benefits**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL (DMEPOS PA RFI)
- **Position:** Support (automation)
- **Rationale:** Automation can improve efficiency and patient access through: automated identification of PAR requirements; real-time completeness checks; structured documentation exchange; real-time electronic visibility of request status; reduction of avoidable denials from incomplete submissions.
- **Specific request:** Support broader adoption of interoperability standards, API-based connectivity, structured machine-readable policies. Clear definition of ownership across the PA workflow would reduce duplication. Reference June 2025 industry pledge commitments to FHIR-based API standardization and expanded real-time approvals by 2027.

**Topic 3: Technology Gaps in DMEPOS PA**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL (DMEPOS PA RFI)
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** Technology does not fully address: variation in payer policies; inconsistent clinical criteria; fragmented accountability between ordering providers and suppliers. Web portals (partially electronic) have increased faster than fully electronic transactions, perpetuating direct data entry burdens. Utilization management tools (lab benefit managers) are often not well integrated into clinical workflows.
- **Specific request:** Promote interoperability standards and API-based connectivity; define clear ownership across the PA workflow; better integrate utilization management tools into existing workflows.

**Topic 4: Device Manufacturer Access to CMS APIs**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support (expanding access)
- **Rationale:** CMS's finalized PA API policies currently address only payer and provider roles. Medical device manufacturers provide PA support services, are well positioned to leverage APIs to reduce administrative burden on providers, and have established HIPAA-compliant processes to assist patients and providers. As new innovative devices continue to be developed, PA support services will be increasingly needed.
- **Specific request:** CMS should provide a mechanism for medical device manufacturers and other third-party submitters to utilize CMS's patient access and prior authorization APIs to submit PA requests directly on behalf of providers.

**Topic 5: DMEPOS PA – Healthcare Workforce Impact**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL (DMEPOS PA RFI)
- **Position:** Clarify/Modify
- **Rationale:** Manual, fragmented PA workflows contribute to provider/supplier/payer staff burnout through repetitive tasks, frequent policy changes requiring ongoing retraining, and workflows that limit focus on clinical care. U.S. Surgeon General Advisory identified PA as a contributor to health worker burnout.
- **Specific request:** Addressing DMEPOS PA through standardization, automation, and reduced variation would directly advance Administration goals of supporting clinician well-being.

**Topic 6: Open Payments "Failure to Report" Definition – Trade Secret/IP Protection**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** Audit documentation may contain highly sensitive, confidential, and trade secret information. FOIA requests could expose such materials to competitors. Courts have recognized that loss of trade secrets cannot be measured in money damages (once lost, lost forever). Risk to members is highly disproportionate to ~$1.16M CMP per non-compliant entity per audit cycle.
- **Specific request:** CMS should acknowledge audit documents may be subject to FOIA; clarify that it will follow 45 C.F.R. § 5.65(d) predisclosure notification and seek submitter input on FOIA Exemption 4; commit that documentation produced in response to an audit will not be used for other enforcement or prosecution (consistent with similar commitment in Open Payments Original Final Rule).

**Topic 7: Open Payments – Contractor Confidentiality Obligations**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** The proposed rule allows "HHS, CMS, OIG or their designees" to audit books and records. Companies have concerns about disclosure, handling, and safeguarding of proprietary business information by third-party contractors.
- **Specific request:** CMS should clarify what contractual, regulatory, or other protections bind designees handling sensitive audit materials; ensure designees are subject to confidentiality obligations no less protective than those applicable to CMS itself.

**Topic 8: Open Payments – Statutory Authority for CMP on Audit Non-Compliance**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** CMS claims Section 1128G(b)(1)(A) of the Act authorizes CMPs for failure to comply with an audit request. However, that section authorizes CMPs only for failure to submit transparency reporting information under subsection (a) — not for audit compliance. CMS's audit authority derives solely from its own regulations at 42 C.F.R. § 403.912(e). Expanding "failure to report" to encompass audit non-compliance may exceed Congressional intent.
- **Specific request:** CMS should confirm and clarify the legal basis for extending CMP authority to audit non-compliance.

**Topic 9: Open Payments – Good Faith Negotiations**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** The proposed definition grants CMS or designees unilateral authority to determine required documentation and impose CMPs on any entity not producing materials within 30 calendar days. No mechanism for good faith discussions about scope before penalties. This contrasts with HIPAA enforcement where procedural safeguards including subpoena processes and pre-penalty dispute resolution protect regulated parties.
- **Specific request:** The final rule should distinguish between outright refusal to participate in an audit and good faith cooperation requiring additional time or scope negotiation. At minimum, the 30-day deadline should be tolled during periods of good faith cooperation and negotiation.

**Topic 10: Open Payments – Privileged Materials**
- **Provision ID:** OPEN-PAYMENTS-CMP
- **Position:** Oppose/Modify
- **Rationale:** The proposed definition fails to account for documents subject to attorney-client privilege, work-product protection, or other legally recognized protections. A company's withholding of privileged materials would be treated as "failure to report" subject to CMPs.
- **Specific request:** Final rule should expressly exclude privileged and otherwise legally protected materials from the scope of "failure to report" so that good faith assertion of recognized legal protection does not give rise to a CMP.

---

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S57 (define "timely" for Open Payments):** AdvaMed does not focus on defining "timely" per se; rather urges that the 30-day deadline be tolled during good faith negotiations and that good faith cooperation not be equated with "failure to report."
- **S58 (CMP amounts):** Notes the ~$1.16M per-entity CMP exposure is highly disproportionate to the risk of trade secret loss for members; indirectly argues CMP framework is disproportionate.
- **S59 (due process):** Directly addresses due process concerns: no pre-penalty dispute resolution; no mechanism to challenge scope of audit request before CMPs imposed; contrasts unfavorably with HIPAA enforcement procedural safeguards; urges good faith negotiation tolling and explicit privilege protections.
- **S79/S80 (DMEPOS PA RFI):** Extensive response describing current burdens, improvement opportunities, automation benefits, technology gaps, workforce impacts, and request for device manufacturer API access.

---

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Standardize DMEPOS PA documentation requirements and minimum data elements across payers; require machine-readable PA rules.
2. Require payers to provide clear, actionable denial reasons for DMEPOS PA.
3. Define service-level expectations for payer response times for DMEPOS PA.
4. Promote interoperability standards and API-based connectivity for DMEPOS PA; define clear ownership across the PA workflow.
5. Provide mechanism for medical device manufacturers and other third-party submitters to access CMS patient access and prior authorization APIs for PA submissions on behalf of providers.
6. Address DMEPOS PA standardization and automation to support clinician well-being, consistent with Administration's health workforce goals.
7. (Open Payments) Acknowledge audit documents may be subject to FOIA; follow 45 C.F.R. § 5.65(d) predisclosure notification and FOIA Exemption 4 procedures.
8. (Open Payments) Commit that documents produced in audit will not be used for other enforcement or prosecution.
9. (Open Payments) Clarify what contractual and regulatory protections bind designees/contractors handling audit materials.
10. (Open Payments) Confirm and clarify statutory legal basis for extending CMP authority to audit non-compliance.
11. (Open Payments) Create mechanism for good faith negotiations before CMPs imposed; toll 30-day deadline during good faith cooperation and scope negotiations.
12. (Open Payments) Expressly exclude privileged and legally protected materials from "failure to report" definition.

---

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Open Payments "failure to report" definition is legally overreaching and fails to protect trade secrets, privileged materials, and good faith cooperation; DMEPOS PA process is predominantly manual, fragmented, and highly burdensome due to lack of standardization and API connectivity.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Audit document exposure to FOIA could expose trade secrets to competitors; loss of trade secrets irreparable (court precedent cited); CMP exposure ($1.16M per entity) highly disproportionate to trade secret risk; only 35% of medical plans have adopted electronic PA standards (2024 CAQH).
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Fragmented accountability between ordering providers and DMEPOS suppliers; no clear ownership structure across PA workflow; increased portal-based (not fully electronic) PA perpetuates data entry burdens; lab benefit managers not well integrated into clinical workflows; aggregator-style dependencies in NCPDP ecosystem.

---

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** 2024 CAQH Index Report: 35% medical plans adopted electronic PA standard, 43% use payer-specific portal, 22% manual processes; ~$1.16M estimated CMP per non-compliant entity per audit cycle based on CMS's proposed per-record CMP methodology and 3-year lookback.
- **Studies or research referenced:** U.S. Surgeon General Advisory on Health Worker Burnout (HHS, 2022); CAQH 2024 Index Report; June 2025 industry pledge secured by HHS Secretary Kennedy and CMS Administrator Oz; Open Payments Original Final Rule (78 Fed. Reg. 9458).
- **Examples provided:** Court cases establishing irreparability of trade secret loss (N. Atl. Instruments v. Haber; FMC Corp. v. Varco Int'l; Norbrook Labs v. G.C. Hanford); HIPAA enforcement procedural safeguards as favorable contrast to proposed Open Payments framework.

---

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Medical device manufacturers (AdvaMed members including hundreds of small companies with fewer than 20 employees), DMEPOS suppliers, ordering clinicians, patients needing mobility/respiratory/chronic disease management devices, healthcare workers facing burnout
- **Economic implications:** Significant administrative burden on DMEPOS suppliers; financial exposure from dispensing items without authorization; CMP disproportionate to $1.16M per entity compared to irreparable trade secret loss; cost of API connectivity implementation
- **Technical feasibility:** Supports API-based connectivity and automation for DMEPOS; notes web portals are increasing faster than fully electronic transactions (perpetuating burdens); encourages FHIR-based API standards consistent with June 2025 industry pledge
- **Patient care impact:** DMEPOS PA delays particularly harmful for mobility, respiratory function, and chronic disease management needs; automation would improve access to medically necessary items; workforce burnout from PA burden reduces quality clinical care

---

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Mixed (supportive of interoperability/automation goals; strongly opposed to Open Payments CMP definition as drafted)
- **Tone:** Technical, Critical (on Open Payments); Collaborative (on DMEPOS PA)
- **Priority level:** High

---

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Courts have recognized, for example, that the 'loss of trade secrets cannot be measured in money damages' because a 'trade secret once lost is, of course, lost forever.'" - Context: On the disproportionate risk to members from Open Payments audit document exposure via FOIA.

2. "AdvaMed respectfully submits that expanding the definition of 'failure to report' to encompass an entity's failure to produce documents in response to an audit request may extend the CMP authority beyond the scope Congress intended." - Context: Statutory authority challenge to the proposed Open Payments definition.

3. "Medical device manufacturers offering prior authorization support services are well positioned to leverage these APIs to reduce administrative burden on providers and improve patient access to medically necessary items." - Context: Requesting CMS provide API access mechanism for device manufacturers as third-party PA submitters.

4. "Manual, fragmented prior authorization workflows contribute directly to burnout across provider, supplier, and payer teams." - Context: Describing workforce impact of current DMEPOS PA processes.

---

## 12. THEMES

- [ ] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Not a primary concern (focused on RFI responses and Open Payments CMP concerns).

- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Significant financial exposure from dispensing DMEPOS without authorization; CMP disproportionate to trade secret risk; administrative burden of manual PA workflows for suppliers.

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Core DMEPOS theme: manual, fragmented workflows; repetitive tasks; policy variation requiring ongoing retraining; burnout from PA administrative burden. Surgeon General advisory cited.

- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Open Payments section: trade secret/IP protection concerns from FOIA exposure; contractor confidentiality obligations; privilege protection; no less protective safeguards than CMS itself.

- [ ] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - Not specifically addressed.

- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Automation and API connectivity for DMEPOS PA is feasible but requires standardization; only 35% of medical plans have adopted electronic standards; web portals increasing faster than fully electronic; device manufacturer API access needed.

- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not specifically addressed for FHIR/NCPDP standards.

- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - DMEPOS PA delays impede access to mobility, respiratory, chronic disease management items; automation would improve access; manufacturer API access reduces provider burden enabling faster PA.

- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Open Payments section: substantial statutory authority challenge to CMP extension to audit non-compliance; argues CMS overreaches Congressional intent under 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7h(b)(1)(A).

- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - References June 2025 industry pledge; requests device manufacturer API access; notes coordination challenge between ordering providers and DMEPOS suppliers.

- [ ] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Not addressed.

- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports payer transparency on PA requirements and denial reasons; machine-readable PA rules; service-level expectations; real-time status visibility. Also calls for CMS transparency on FOIA/trade secret protections.

- [x] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Mentions hundreds of AdvaMed member companies with fewer than 20 employees; CMP disproportionate risk noted particularly for smaller manufacturers.

- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Central DMEPOS concern: fragmented systems not electronically aligned; unclear ownership between ordering provider and DMEPOS supplier; web portals perpetuating data entry burdens; lab benefit managers not integrated.

- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Device manufacturer role in PA process unaddressed by current API framework; requests third-party submitter access; references aggregator-style ecosystem complexity.
